secondaryObjectives: Formulating mathematical models from real-world scenarios

sources.cite: OpenStax, Biology, 45.3 Environmental Limits to Population Growth
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch. Exponential growth assumes unlimited resources and gives a J-shaped curve; in logistic growth the rate slows as the population nears the carrying capacity K and levels off in an S-shaped curve. The case applies the same model choice to adoption in a fixed population (author's application).
Every organization, person, count and deadline is invented teaching data; tool output is an authored rendering in the tool style.

brief.situation: You built adoption_forecast.py for Millbrook Public Library (fictional). It fits an exponential curve to the first eight weeks of app sign-ups and projects to June: 120,000 users. The service area has 40,000 residents, and weekly growth has started to slow. The license tier is signed at 11:00. It is 10:05.
handover: Seat tiers: up to 15,000; up to 30,000; 100,000+.

Each step takes working minutes, and the clock moves by the minutes it takes. The deadline runs on the same clock.
Shipping is final for this case. Afterwards you record what you found and explain your reasoning.

scoring.modelReasoning: A forecast three times the town's population means the model's assumption is wrong. Exponential growth assumes a constant rate with no limit, but the weekly rate has fallen from 56% to 15% as the pool of residents is used up. A logistic model with a carrying capacity fits the slowing growth and predicts held-out weeks within 4%, putting June near 14,000. Capping the exponential still overshoots; refitting recent weeks keeps the constant-growth assumption.
